title: My family
goal: Talk about your family — and, along the way, put vowel harmony into your own hands, because almost every family word needs a suffix.
bekal: name family members and say how many there are
use *манай* and *танай* — two words Mongolians use every day
pick the right suffix vowel without opening a table

notes: ⚠️ **Манай isn't "we" but "our" — and Mongolians use it where English says "my".** *Манай гэр бүл* is literally "our family", but it means "my family". Saying *миний гэр бүл* sounds cold, as if your family were your property. Think of how English speakers say "our house" even when talking alone.

**Танай is its polite partner**: "your", used for the other person's family, home, office, country. *Танай гэр бүл*, *танай улс*, *танай компани*. It's one of the most frequent words in polite conversation.

**Маань and тань stick to the end of a noun** and mean "my/our …" and "your …". *Аав **маань*** = my father; *ээж **тань*** = your mother. This is warmer than *миний аав*, and it's almost always used for family members.

⚠️ **Mongolian distinguishes older brother from older sister, but not younger siblings.** *Ах* = older brother, *эгч* = older sister, *дүү* = younger sibling (either sex). To be specific: *эрэгтэй дүү* (younger brother), *эмэгтэй дүү* (younger sister). English splits by sex instead of by age — Mongolian splits by age first.

**The suffix -тай / -тэй / -той that appears ten times in this dialogue means "having".** *Хүнтэй* = "with people", *настай* = "aged", *хүүхэдтэй* = "with children". It's the main way Mongolian expresses having, and Unit 15 covers it fully. For now, take it as a pattern: **noun + -тай = having that noun.**

grammars.title: Choosing the suffix vowel: vowel harmony in your own hands
body: This is the first place you really have to use the rule from the front pages. The suffix *-тай* has three faces, and the **last vowel** of the base word decides which.

head: Last vowel of the base word
Suffix
Example
Meaning

after: Notice that **о** gets its own suffix (*-той*), while **ө** goes with the front group (*-тэй*). It's the only extra complication beyond the two-group split, and it applies to every suffix with a vowel, not just *-тай*.

**Test it with your ear, not the table.** Say *номтой* and *номтэй* out loud. The second feels like tripping, because your mouth has to jump from the back group to the front group mid-word. That's all vowel harmony really is: a mouth that refuses to jump.

grammars.title: Saying your age — and why there's no verb
body: Mongolian gives age with no verb at all. The pattern is **number + нас + -тай**, literally "having so many years".
after: ⚠️ Numbers before a noun use **the form ending in -н**: *хорь* → *хорин*, *гурав* → *гурван*, *тав* → *таван*, *долоо* → *долоон*. The bare form (*хорь*, *гурав*) is used only when the number stands alone: *Хэд вэ?* — *Гурав.*

**Asking an older person's age is not considered rude in Mongolia**, unlike in many Western countries. Questions about age, marital status, and number of children are a normal part of a first meeting.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Ах* and *эгч* are used far more widely than their literal meaning. You call an older waitress *эгч ээ*, a taxi driver *ах аа*, and a middle-aged neighbor *ах*. It's a bit like calling people "sir" or "ma'am", but warmer — and addressing someone by their bare name with no title can feel cold.

blocks.title: The suffix -аа for calling someone
items: The vowel follows harmony: *аав* (back group) → *аа*; *ээж* (front group) → *ээ*.
⚠️ Without this suffix, calling someone sounds like mentioning them, not calling them. Compare "Mom" in a sentence with "Mo-om!" across the house.

blocks.text: Notice the suffixes **-ч** and **-чин** in *жолооч*, *малчин*, *тогооч*, *худалдагч*. They mean "a person who does" — just like English "-er". *Мал* (livestock) → *малчин* (herder); *тогоо* (pot) → *тогооч* (cook). Once you recognize these suffixes, you can guess dozens of job names yourself.

blocks.title: Six questions that always come up
items: *Танай гэр бүл хэдэн хүнтэй вэ?* — How many people are in your family?
*Та хэдэн настай вэ?* — How old are you?
*Ах дүү хэдүүлээ вэ?* — How many siblings are you?
*Танайх хаана байдаг вэ?* — Where does your family live?

blocks.text: ⚠️ The answer to the fifth question uses a special form: *Бид гурвуулаа* ("the three of us"), *дөрвүүлээ* (the four of us), *тавуулаа* (the five of us). The suffix **-уулаа / -үүлээ** means "all together, so many people"; English needs a whole phrase for it.

A useful cultural note: in Mongolia, **questions about family are not small talk**. People really want to know, and a one-word answer feels closed off. If you're asked how many siblings you have, also mention where they live and what they do — just two extra sentences are enough to turn a formal conversation into a warm one.

items: There are five people in my family.
My mother works at a school.
How many people are in your family?
